title: The Council Votes

pages.text:
*The Handbook of Small Truths, Entry 16: A truth told in time is a gift. A truth told late is a bill.*

The Council Hall smelled of old varnish and anxiety. It was dawn, or what passed for dawn in Drum One, where the window-boxes on the rim had been programmed to dim from a polite amber to a respectful grey. The room was full. Not just full, but packed in the way that implies everyone had stopped thinking about personal space and started thinking about oxygen. Every bench was occupied, the balcony rail was lined with shoulders, and the stairs were a solid staircase of legs and knees. Kess stood in the center of the floor, her silver-streaked curls bouncing slightly as she shifted her weight. She felt like a seed dropped into a very large, very quiet pot.

Chief Engineer Bram Voss sat in the front row. He was wearing his coverall, the grey one with the red wrench badge, but he had washed it. It was a different shade of grey, a cleaner, more official grey that seemed to make his ginger beard look even bushier. He was polishing the badge with a rag, a nervous tic that usually meant he was about to break something. Beside him, Dr. Imani Brandt sat with her hands folded in her lap, her white hair close-cropped and severe, her gold spectacles catching the light. She looked like a rock in a river, small and immovable.

Councilor Dara Hale sat at the head of the long table. Her auburn hair was pinned in its neat bun, her charcoal tunic buttoned to the throat. She looked tired. Not the kind of tired that sleep fixes, but the kind that comes from carrying a secret for too long. She looked at Kess, and for a moment, their eyes met. Hale’s expression was unreadable, a flat line of resignation. Kess took a breath. The air in the hall was still. It was the kind of silence that happens before a pump kicks on, a held breath that waits for the pressure to build.

Kess looked at the faces. Some were hopeful. Some were skeptical. One boy in the back row was eating a pear. She looked at Voss, who had stopped polishing and was now staring at the floor. She looked at Brandt, who was watching her with an intensity that felt like a heat lamp. She looked at Hale, who was waiting.

"Good morning," Kess said. Her voice came out steady, though her throat felt tight. "Thank you for coming."

The Hall did not cheer. It did not applaud. It listened.
pages.image: A packed council hall with wooden benches and a high balcony, crowded with people; a young woman with curly black hair and a green coverall stands in the center, while a man in a grey coverall and an elderly woman in a grey cardigan sit in the front row, looking tense.

pages.text:
Kess walked to the front of the room, her sneakers making a soft, rhythmic tap on the polished wood. She did not use the podium. She set the tablet on the table, leaving it there, because she wanted the hall to hear the sound of her voice, not the sterile echo of a speaker. Her eyes swept the Council, then the packed benches, settling on the faces that had come to judge her.

"The power margin is three point one percent," she said. "That is the number Tally gave us. It represents the gap between what we consume and what we can safely reject as heat. It is not a lot. It is the thickness of a fingernail. If we cut the orchard lights, we gain that margin. But we lose the trees."

A low murmur rippled through the hall, and someone in the back row coughed into their sleeve.

"I have spent the last fifteen days looking at the numbers," Kess continued, her voice steady despite the tightness in her throat. "I have examined the thermal maps. I have analyzed the flow rates. And I found something." She paused, letting the silence stretch. She looked directly at Voss. "There is a leak."

Voss looked up. His face drained of color, the red wrench badge on his coverall suddenly looking very small against his pale skin.

"It is not a large leak," Kess said. "It is a micro-leak in the radiator loop. It has been there for years. It is slow. It is tiny. But it is stealing the heat rejection capacity. That is why the margin is down. That is why Tally is worried."

She turned her gaze to Hale. "I am not certain this will work. I am certain, however, that not trying is certain to fail. We can fix the leak. We can seal it. We can test it. But we have to do it now, before the next winter, before the margin drops below one percent."

The hall was silent. The quality of the silence had changed. It was no longer the held breath of anticipation, but the sharp, waiting quiet of a question. Kess felt the pressure of it, a physical weight in her chest, though she expected anger. She had not expected this. She felt small, dwarfed by the scale of the ship and the crowd, but she did not feel alone.

"There is a risk," she said. "The repair requires a spacewalk. It is dangerous. It is tight. But it is possible. I have the plan. I have the tools. I have the team. I just need the permission."
pages.image: A young woman in a green coverall stands at the front of a wooden council table, addressing a silent crowd; her expression is serious and determined, while a man in the front row looks up with a shocked, pale face.

pages.text:
"Excuse me."

The voice cut through the stale air with the precise, jagged snap of a grafting knife severing a dead limb. Ferris Quill rose from the second row, a tall, angular man whose face seemed carved from the same hard timber as the Council benches. He wore the blue tunic of the maintenance guild, a garment that usually smelled of ozone and grease, but here it looked stiff and official. His eyes, fixed on Kess, held the cold, unyielding intensity of flint.

"Why was the Council not informed?" he asked, his tone flat and dangerous. "We have sat in this hall for years, watching the margins erode. Why did the data flow to the minds but not to the minds that must vote? Why the secrecy?"

The murmur in the hall died instantly, leaving a vacuum that felt thicker than the recycled air. Kess opened her mouth to deflect, to pivot toward the technical details, but Councilor Hale was already rising.

She moved with the slow, deliberate care of someone handling a cracked instrument. She smoothed the front of her charcoal tunic, a perfunctory gesture that did nothing to steady the slight tremor in her hands. Her gaze swept the assembly, pausing on Quill before settling, finally, on Kess.

"I am responsible," Hale said.

Her voice was low, stripped of its usual bureaucratic polish, yet it carried to the upper balcony where a boy paused mid-bite of a pear, his eyes widening in the dim light. He stopped chewing, the fruit halfway to his mouth, and stared.

"I chose delay," Hale continued, her words landing with the heavy, irreversible thud of a dropped wrench. "I chose silence. I was afraid. I feared that if we admitted the weakness, we would be forced to act, and I was not certain we possessed the tools or the time to succeed."

The silence in the room shifted again, losing its hostile edge and gaining a strange, fragile quality, like the tension in a string just before it sings. Hale looked at Kess, and for the first time, a small, tired smile touched her lips, a thin crack in the armor of her authority.

"I was wrong to fear the truth," she said. "I move to lift Directive Nine. I move to authorize the EVA. I move to give Kess Adair the permission she needs."
pages.image: A woman in a charcoal tunic stands at the head of a council table, her hands resting on the wood, her expression solemn and weary; a tall man in a blue tunic stands nearby, looking confrontational, while the crowd watches in silence.

pages.text:
The vote was not a rush, nor was it a cheer; it was a procedure, slow and deliberate as the turning of a large gear. Council members stood, or raised a hand, or nodded with the careful precision of a mechanic checking a bolt. The count dragged on while Kess stood at the front, her hands at her sides, watching the faces and the rising palms. She did not count them, nor did she need to, for she felt the room’s balance shifting, the air in the hall tightening and then releasing, the way pressure in a pump loop changes just before the flow steadies.

Tally’s lamp-panel glowed amber, a soft, warm pulse in the dim hall, steady as the hum of the grow-lights in the Orchard.

"Thirty-one for," Tally said, its voice smooth and clear. "Nine against. Two abstaining."

The hall exhaled, a collective release of long-held tension finally letting go. A cheer broke out from the balcony, not a roar but a burst of sound, a sudden, bright explosion of joy. People clapped and shouted, while a woman in the front row started crying, her hands covering her mouth as the sound washed over her.

Pim was on the stairs, leaning on the railing with his yellow-tied puffs of hair bouncing as he shouted.

"I TOLD you it was suspicious!" he yelled. "I TOLD you the pages were missing!"

Seven people around him tried to hush him, putting their hands over his mouth and attempting to pull him down the stairs, but Pim did not stop. He was grinning, shining with the fierce, unyielding pride of a twelve-year-old who had won.

Kess looked at the balcony, where she saw Lio standing with his navy jumpsuit bright against the wood. He was not cheering; he was watching, his face calm but his eyes bright, and he nodded to her with a small, quiet gesture. Kess felt a smile spread across her face, not a big one, but a small, quiet smile that was real.
pages.image: A crowded council hall with people cheering and clapping; a small boy in a red hoodie stands on the stairs, shouting and grinning, while a tall boy in a navy jumpsuit stands on the balcony, watching with a calm expression.

pages.text:
Hale did not sit. She remained standing at the head of the table, her palms flat against the polished wood, grounding herself in the grain. Her silver-streaked auburn bun was still, but her eyes, tired and kind, moved directly to Kess. There was no ceremony in her posture, only the quiet, deliberate stillness of a woman who had spent years holding a fragile balance.

"The orchard’s lights will not be cut," she said, her voice steady and clear, cutting through the residual hum of the crowd. "Instead, the Orchard will dim by half for the duration of the repair. It is a shared sacrifice, a choice we make together, not a verdict handed down from above. And then, when the repair is done, the lights will be restored. Full power. Full sun."

The words hung in the air, concrete and manageable. It was not a complete victory, nor was it a perfect solution, but it was a choice, a truth they could hold without breaking.

"I agree," Kess said.

Brandt, standing beside her, squeezed her arm. It was a gentle, firm pressure, warm and reassuring, the kind of touch that said *you did that* without needing to speak the words. Brandt leaned in, her voice low, almost a whisper, her gold spectacles catching the amber light from Tally’s lamp-panel.

"Now it is a ship that tells itself the truth," she murmured.

Kess looked out at the hall, at the faces that had just voted, at the amber glow of Tally’s lamp pulsing softly in the dimness. The gravity of the moment settled over her, not as a burden, but as a responsibility, a new weight she was already learning to carry. She was not just a gardener anymore, not just a girl with a tool-belt and soil under her fingernails. She was part of the ship, part of the truth, a thread in the vast, intricate weave of their survival.

And the truth was simple, terrifying, and beautiful: they could fix it. They could save the trees. They could save the ship.
